title: From Michelin Stars to Street Rolls: Indian Restaurants Claim New American Ground
excerpt: A wave of openings — from a James Beard semifinalist in Phoenix to Kolkata street food in Jersey City — signals that Indian cuisine's US expansion is accelerating faster than ever.
body:
Something is happening across America's dining map this summer, and it smells like roasted spices and fresh-pressed roti.

In the span of a single week, no fewer than five Indian restaurants announced openings or expansions in cities that, a decade ago, barely had a curry house. From a Michelin-recognised chef heading to suburban Phoenix to a 24-year-old Kolkata street-food favourite crossing the Hudson River, the wave is as diverse as India's own regional cuisines — and it's reaching places the diaspora has long called home without the restaurants to match.

## The Michelin Connection Heads West

The biggest name in the wave belongs to Sujan Sarkar, the chef behind Chicago's Michelin-starred Indienne. His regional Indian concept NADU — meaning "homeland" — earned a Michelin Bib Gourmand and a James Beard Award semifinalist nod for Best New Restaurant within months of its Chicago debut in 2025. Now it's heading to Desert Ridge Marketplace in Phoenix, partnering with Zest Hospitality Group to bring Kashmiri roganjosh, Benne masala dosa, and Kerala-style beef ularthiyathu to the Arizona desert.

The Phoenix location, which will seat more than 120 guests, will be led by Executive Chef Pujan Sarkar, who also oversees the Michelin-recognised Tiya in San Francisco. The restaurant will feature artwork by Chicago-based artist Abhay Sehgal and a cocktail programme built on turmeric, kokum, vetiver, and Indian whiskies. An opening date hasn't been announced, but the fit-out is under way.

## Kolkata Street Food Crosses the River

Meanwhile, on the East Coast, The Kati Roll Company is finally bringing its iconic Kolkata-style rolls to New Jersey. Founded in 2002 by Payal Saha in Manhattan's Greenwich Village, the brand helped introduce Americans to kati rolls — grilled fillings wrapped inside fresh roti or paratha — long before fast-casual Indian was a category anyone tracked.

The Jersey City outpost, opening July 1 at 924 Bergen Avenue near the Journal Square PATH station, joins four NYC locations plus outposts in Dallas and London. Founder Anil Bathwal has plans for additional NJ locations in Hoboken, Metuchen, and New Brunswick before the year is out. "New Jersey customers have been crossing the river to find us for years," Bathwal told NorthJersey.com. "It felt right to finally come to them."

## From Mumbai to Manhattan's East Village

In New York, chef Aarthi Sampath has opened Drāvida, a restaurant that traces the migration routes of South Asian food across continents. A winner of both Chopped and Beat Bobby Flay, Sampath came to the US from Mumbai in 2013 and built her debut restaurant around the idea that Indian cuisine doesn't stop at India's borders.

The menu at Drāvida features Trinidad's beloved Doubles, South Africa's Oxtail Bunny Chow, and the Nasi Kandar Feast — a hearty Indo-Malay rice spread. A hidden 20-seat speakeasy called Jam and Jaggery sits upstairs. The concept is as much an argument about diaspora identity as it is a dinner reservation.

## The Quieter Expansions

The openings aren't all celebrity-chef affairs. In Fort Collins, Colorado, Saiprasad and Sunita Palusa have expanded their decade-old Bawarchi Biryanis into a second location inside the Hilton Garden Inn, opening it to the public with a 15% discount through June 30. And in Newburgh, New York — deep in the Hudson Valley — The 100 Food Journey launched its official grand opening with a concept that cycles its entire menu every 100 days, each cycle devoted to a different region of India.

## Why It Matters for the Diaspora

For NRIs who settled in second-tier cities and college towns decades ago, the expansion is personal. For years, the only option was a drive to the nearest metro area or cooking from scratch. Now, the restaurants are following the people — into suburbs, into hotel lobbies, into strip malls on Bergen Avenue.

According to Datassential, 49% of US consumers have eaten at an Indian restaurant, and Technomic data shows 52% have tried Indian food and liked it. Those numbers have been climbing steadily, fuelled by grocery chains like Trader Joe's making paneer tikka masala and vegetable biryani pantry staples. But the real shift isn't in the numbers. It's in the geography. Indian restaurants aren't just opening — they're opening *everywhere*.
